parsed_answer.content:
Polymorphism, literally translating to 'many forms', is a foundational pillar of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in Java that allows a single interface to represent different underlying forms (data types). In enterprise Java applications, polymorphism decouples the 'what' from the 'how', enabling code to be extensible, maintainable, and loosely coupled. Rather than relying on rigid conditional logic or concrete implementations, developers can write generalized routines that operate against abstract contracts.

Java implements polymorphism in two distinct flavors: compile-time polymorphism (static binding) and runtime polymorphism (dynamic binding). Compile-time polymorphism is achieved primarily through method overloading, where multiple methods share the exact same identifier within a class but possess distinct method signatures—differing in parameter count, type, or ordering. The Java compiler resolves these calls during compilation by evaluating the static types provided at the call site. Conversely, runtime polymorphism is realized through method overriding and interface implementation, where a reference variable of a supertype can point to an object of a subtype. The exact method implementation to execute is deferred until the program runs, resolved dynamically by the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) using the actual runtime type of the object rather than its declared reference type.

items: During runtime polymorphism, the JVM utilizes method tables (vtables) allocated per loaded class in the metaspace to locate the precise memory address of an overridden method efficiently.

When an instance method is called on a polymorphic reference, the JVM emits the `invokevirtual` bytecode instruction, which inspects the object header's class pointer to resolve the receiver type dynamically.

Field shadowing and static methods do not exhibit runtime polymorphism in Java; instance fields and static methods are resolved strictly based on the compile-time reference type, leading to potential pitfalls if developers confuse variable hiding with overriding.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap with runtime polymorphism involves attempting to override static methods or access inherited instance fields. Because static methods are bound at compile-time to the reference type, declaring a static method with the same signature in a subclass results in 'method hiding', not overriding. If you invoke a static method through a parent reference pointing to a child instance, the parent's version executes, bypassing your subclass logic entirely and introducing subtle bugs that static analysis tools like SonarQube often flag.

title: What is polymorphism in Java? (compile-time vs runtime)
